summary: Specifies GRE procedures for IPv6, used as either the payload or the delivery protocol. Earlier GRE procedures were defined only for IPv4.

eli5.summary: GRE can wrap one kind of packet in another. This teaches it to work with the newer addresses.

subtitle: The rules for running GRE tunnels when IPv6 is the payload, the delivery network, or both.

tldr.problem: GRE can carry any network-layer protocol over any other, but its procedures were only specified for IPv4 as payload or delivery protocol, not for IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC leaves the GRE header format alone and adds IPv6 rules: Protocol Type 0x86DD for IPv6 payloads, Next Header 47 for IPv6 delivery, a 1280-octet tunnel check, and guidance on checksums and fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: Vendors' existing IPv6 GRE behavior gets a written standard, with a warning that GRE over IPv6 must only be deployed where the checksum risk is judged acceptable.

sections.title: Introduction and Terms
sections.content:
Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) carries any network-layer payload protocol over any network-layer delivery protocol. Its procedures were specified for IPv4 only. This document specifies them for IPv6, used as payload or delivery protocol, and like RFC 2784 it describes how GRE has been implemented by several vendors.

Key terms: the GRE delivery header is the IPv4 or IPv6 header whose addresses are the GRE ingress and egress nodes. The GRE overhead is the delivery header plus the GRE header, in octets. The GRE MTU (GMTU) is the largest packet a tunnel can carry without fragmentation of any kind: the path MTU between ingress and egress minus the GRE overhead.
sections.eli5: The outer envelope has its own address, the inner letter has another, and the envelope takes up some room, so the letter inside has to be a bit smaller.

sections.title: GRE Header and the Checksum Bit
sections.content:
The GRE header format and the behaviors of RFC 2784 and RFC 2890 are unchanged. The one thing the RFC adds is advice on the Checksum Present field: the ingress node SHOULD set it to zero, though implementations MAY offer a configuration option to set it to one.

If it is one, the egress node MUST use the GRE Checksum to verify the header and payload. Zero saves computation, and the GRE Checksum is often partly redundant with the IPv4, TCP or UDP checksums. But with zero, the GRE header has no checksum protection, and parts of the payload may have none either. Operators are told to evaluate the risks and configure ingress nodes accordingly.
sections.eli5: A check number on the outer envelope is usually skipped because the letter inside often has its own. Skipping it is cheaper, but sometimes nothing checks the envelope.

sections.title: IPv6 as the GRE Payload
sections.content:
When the tunnel carries IPv6, the GRE Protocol Type MUST be Ether Type 0x86DD.

A tunnel MUST be able to carry a 1280-octet IPv6 packet from ingress to egress without fragmenting the payload. Any tunnel with a GMTU of 1280 octets or more meets this, as do tunnels that can fragment and reassemble delivery packets. Before activating a tunnel, and periodically afterwards, the ingress node MUST verify this ability and activate or deactivate the tunnel accordingly. The RFC suggests sending a 1280-octet IPv6 packet addressed to itself through the tunnel. Many existing implementations do not do this check, so unless the GMTU is guaranteed to exceed 1280 they MUST be configured so the endpoints can fragment and reassemble the delivery packet.

If a payload packet fits within the GMTU, it is encapsulated with no fragmentation of either packet. If it is larger and the GMTU is at least 1280, the ingress MUST discard it and send an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message to the source, with the MTU field set to the GMTU. If it is larger and the GMTU is under 1280, the ingress MUST encapsulate the whole packet and fragment the delivery header so the egress can reassemble it.
sections.eli5: Every tunnel must be wide enough for one standard-size box. If a box is too big, it is sent back with a note saying how big is allowed.

sections.title: IPv6 as the GRE Delivery Protocol
sections.content:
With IPv6 delivery, the GRE header MAY follow the delivery header directly, or IPv6 extension headers MAY sit between them. In the first case the IPv6 Next Header field MUST be 47; otherwise the last extension header's Next Header MUST be 47.

By default, the ingress node cannot fragment the IPv6 delivery header and the egress node cannot reassemble it. Implementations MAY offer optional configuration to allow either.
sections.eli5: The outer envelope has a label saying 'a GRE letter is inside', and that label is the number 47.

sections.title: The Checksum Gap with IPv6 Delivery
sections.content:
The GRE checksum cannot detect corruption of the IPv6 delivery header, and IPv6 has no header checksum of its own. So no checksum can catch a corrupted delivery header.

If the destination address is corrupted, the packet reaches the wrong node, which will drop it, decapsulate and forward it correctly, or decapsulate and forward it to the wrong place. The last is unacceptable. It requires that both nodes be VPN Provider Edge routers, with VPNs on both that use overlapping address space such as that of RFC 1918, and matching state on both. The RFC calls this extremely unlikely, but one misdelivered packet can harm applications, and leaking across VPNs is a security breach.

Authenticating the payload end to end could mitigate it. GRE over IPv6 MUST NOT be deployed except where the operator deems the risk acceptable.
sections.eli5: If the outer address gets smudged, the envelope could go to the wrong office. Almost always that office sends it on or throws it away, but in a rare case it could be delivered to the wrong person.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats that RFC 4023 identifies for MPLS over GRE apply to any GRE payload. They can be mitigated by authenticating or encrypting the delivery packet with IPsec. When the payload is IPv6, the payload itself can be authenticated or encrypted with IPsec instead. Otherwise, this specification adds no security considerations beyond those of RFC 2784.

The RFC points to RFC 4942 for IPv6 security in general and to RFC 6169 for tunnel security concerns.
sections.eli5: To keep the mail private, lock the inner letter or the outer envelope with a strong lock.
